vignette: John is a 25-year-old African American journalist who has been struggling with significant psychological distress since an encounter with police that left him deeply traumatized. The event began when he was investigating a story late at night in a part of the city known for heavy police presence. As he walked back to his car, footsteps echoed behind him, and before he could react, officers rushed towards him, mistaking him for someone else involved in an altercation nearby. Despite John’s attempts to explain, he was detained, handcuffed, and questioned aggressively. The experience left him shaken, with the memory of those footsteps still haunting him. John's symptoms began shortly after this event. Whenever he hears footsteps behind or near him, it triggers intense anxiety, sending a wave of fear through his body. He avoids areas where such sounds might occur, wearing concealing clothing to avoid being noticed and steering clear of locations that remind him of the incident. The sound of certain songs from his car radio also triggers vivid memories of that night, making him feel as if he is reliving it all over again. These triggers have led John to adopt maladaptive strategies such as avoiding anything that could potentially cause negative or positive feelings and concealing clothing to blend into the background. He has become particularly sensitive to auditory cues, frequently glancing behind him to check for anyone following him. The fear of being in unfamiliar places exacerbates this behavior since he cannot assess the danger accurately. John's memories of the event feel more real and vivid than other memories; he often hears the sounds from that night replaying in his head. When he tries to recount what happened, he frequently loses track of his thoughts, unable to articulate a coherent narrative. This inability to explain clearly amplifies his sense of isolation and distress. John has come to believe that his life has been irrevocably altered by this trauma. He feels a profound sense of loss and misery, convinced that the incident destroyed any chance he had at happiness. The memory of being falsely accused and mistreated haunts him daily, leading him to question his ability to continue working as a journalist, an identity that once defined him. The negative appraisals further fuel his maladaptive strategies. John’s belief that his life is ruined makes him more prone to avoiding situations where he might be reminded of the trauma or experience similar emotions. This avoidance has extended into his work environment; he no longer feels comfortable investigating stories in high-risk areas, limiting his professional opportunities and causing a rift with colleagues who do not fully understand his situation. John’s negative appraisals also exacerbate his threat monitoring behaviors. He is hyper-vigilant about auditory cues and frequently checks behind him to ensure safety. The vividness of his memories contributes to these anxieties, making it difficult for him to concentrate on tasks at hand. His attempts to avoid all feelings have led to a numbing effect where he struggles to engage with the world around him. What frightens John most is the fear that he will never recover from this trauma and that his life as he knew it is over. He hopes that seeking help might provide some relief and rekindle the sense of happiness and purpose he once had. The combination of these symptoms has taken a toll on both his personal and professional life, pushing him to finally reach out for support.
